direct.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.
Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

concepts.name: user-centered design
concepts.definition: User-centered design (UCD) is a design approach in which users are actively or passively involved in the overall design lifecycle, and the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, ideally from the users' point of view rather than the programmer's convenience, to build a usable application.

defining_facts.text: The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces.
The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability.

Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.
The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable.

User-centered design (UCD), also called user-centric or human-centric design, is a design approach in which the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view rather than by the programmer's convenience.

concepts.name: requirement gathering
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering is a stage of the interactive system development lifecycle that collects functional and non-functional requirements from clients and end users, focuses on end-user usability requirements, and specifies them for design, implementation, and deployment.

defining_facts.text: In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.
Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.
The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

concepts.name: interface design
concepts.definition: Interface design is an activity in interactive system development that involves designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle, repeated with prototyping and quick evaluation until stable, and is separate from code design.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

never_defined.name: hardware
never_defined.definition: Hardware is a part of an extended reality (XR) system, including input devices, output devices, processing devices, central processing units, graphics processing units, and memory.

never_defined.name: software
never_defined.definition: Software is a resource in extended reality that is used to process input data, generate output data, and create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.

never_defined.name: feature
never_defined.definition: A Feature is a unique, already present part of a natural environment, such as a point, corner, or line intersection, that is detected and distinguished by descriptors to estimate camera pose.

never_defined.name: user interface
never_defined.definition: A user interface is an interface whose design and qualities make it usable, and where usability issues arise.

never_defined.name: deployment
never_defined.definition: Deployment is the development stage in which a built system is made available, either as a native application requiring tailored software development kits or as a web application that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

never_defined.name: mobile platform
never_defined.definition: Mobile platform is a deployment platform, typically meaning the operating system plus hardware, such as Android or iOS.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: System design is the part of interactive system development in which user characteristics, usability requirements, and observed user activities are used to plan system features.

never_defined.name: task
never_defined.definition: A task is an activity that users perform, involving a sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes, and whose performance data can be used to evaluate an interface.

never_defined.name: context of use
never_defined.definition: Context of use is the specific usage scenario or work setting in which users perform tasks with a product, with respect to which its usability is defined.

never_defined.name: client requirement
never_defined.definition: Client requirement is a requirement other than an end-user requirement, which the requirement gathering stage in an interactive system development life cycle concerns.

never_defined.name: requirement specification
never_defined.definition: Requirement specification is required for system implementation.

never_defined.name: system implementation
never_defined.definition: System implementation is a process for which a requirement specification is required.

never_defined.name: programming language
never_defined.definition: Programming language is used to develop an application, with Java or JavaScript as examples.

never_defined.name: Java
never_defined.definition: Java is a programming language that can be used to develop an application for a mobile platform.

never_defined.name: JavaScript
never_defined.definition: JavaScript is a programming language that can be used to develop an application for a mobile platform.

never_defined.name: feasibility stage
never_defined.definition: The feasibility stage is the stage related to decisions in requirement gathering about a mobile platform and programming language, rather than to end-user usability requirements.

never_defined.name: relational database management system
never_defined.definition: A relational database management system (RDBMS) is a tool that can be used for storing information.

never_defined.name: my structured query language
never_defined.definition: My structured query language is a relational database management system (RDBMS) tool.

never_defined.name: design stage
never_defined.definition: Design stage is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle that may involve interface design or code design.

never_defined.name: quality attribute
never_defined.definition: A quality attribute is an attribute of software that non-functional requirements are typically related to.

never_defined.name: performance-related requirement
never_defined.definition: Performance-related requirement is a category of non-functional requirements.

never_defined.name: operating constraint
never_defined.definition: An operating constraint is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

never_defined.name: economic consideration
never_defined.definition: Economic consideration is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

never_defined.name: lifecycle requirement
never_defined.definition: Lifecycle requirement is one of the categories of non-functional requirements.

never_defined.name: phenomenological research method
never_defined.definition: Phenomenological research method is the term used to highlight the importance of contextual inquiry in user-centered design.

never_defined.name: interview
never_defined.definition: Interview is the part of contextual inquiry that may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify behaviors or activities, and it is used to gather usability requirements and identify user groups.

never_defined.name: observation
never_defined.definition: Observation is a part of contextual inquiry in which people in their natural work settings are observed and data are recorded, enabling designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints.

never_defined.name: user behavior
never_defined.definition: User behavior is the way users perform tasks in a specific work context, and knowing it is essential to ensure usability and gather insight about end-user requirements.

never_defined.name: task domain
never_defined.definition: Task domain is something about which designers gather knowledge by observing and interacting with users in contextual inquiry to support design decisions.

never_defined.name: work culture
never_defined.definition: Work culture is one of the things that contextual inquiry enables designers to learn about.

never_defined.name: physical constraint
never_defined.definition: Physical constraint is one kind of constraint at the workplace.

never_defined.name: social constraint
never_defined.definition: A social constraint is one of the workplace constraints that designers can learn about through contextual inquiry, which supports design decisions.

never_defined.name: design decision
never_defined.definition: A design decision is a decision in design that is supported by contextual inquiry, in which observations and interaction with users help designers learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace.

never_defined.name: system development
never_defined.definition: System development is an area in which contextual inquiry is important for studying users and enabling design refinement.

never_defined.name: design refinement
never_defined.definition: Design refinement is something that contextual inquiry enables in system development.

never_defined.name: user activities
never_defined.definition: User activities are the activities of users that contextual inquiry observes and that a system design must support as features to be usable.

never_defined.name: calendar app
never_defined.definition: A calendar app is a scheduling application for managerial staff that supports setting meeting dates and reminders and checking day-wise or overall schedules.
